title: Documented cleaning schedules and outsourced cleaning
audience: Cleaning supervisors, contract cleaners and staff who work to a written cleaning schedule.
learningOutcomes: Describe the content a written cleaning schedule has to include.
List the four elements an outsourced cleaning service must document.
Explain how a schedule is altered when one particular microbe is present.

instruction.heading: What the schedule must contain
instruction.body: Every healthcare organisation should hold a written cleaning schedule. It names who is responsible for each task, sets out the roster, states how often each area or item is cleaned, and lists the product to use for each area. Staff also need education and training that matches their tasks, covering both routine and special cleaning.

instruction.heading: Outsourced cleaning
instruction.body: A contract cleaner must set down how the work will be performed. That document covers four headings: how often and how each task is done; who works the roster, from permanent and part-time staff to relief workers and supervisors; what supplies and equipment are provided, including fluids and paper goods; and how the contractor manages the service on the ground. The B5.1 table offers a benchmark other settings may tailor.

instruction.heading: Changing the schedule for a known organism
instruction.body: Every infection risk gets weighed, and the timetable changes whenever a known microbe is in the building. The guideline's illustration involves Clostridium difficile: surfaces get a detergent wash followed by hypochlorite. The illustration makes the point; the strength, mixing and wait time are set by the product label and the facility's approved instruction.

instruction.heading: Local adjustment
instruction.body: The frequency table is a yardstick, not a law for every site. Each facility drafts its own timetable that fits its setting, then checks how that timetable performs. If the timetable seems wrong for your room, tell your supervisor in writing. Never alter a frequency or a product by yourself.

procedure: Find the current schedule for your area and confirm its issue date.
Read the frequency and the product recorded for each item you clean.
Check the roster to confirm who is responsible for each task on your shift.
Note any outbreak or organism alert and check whether the schedule has been changed for it.
Record completed tasks against the schedule as you go, not from memory.
Raise any gap between the schedule and the area's real needs with your supervisor, in writing.

workedExamples.situation: You are a contract cleaner. A notice says a ward is managing a suspected C. difficile outbreak, but your schedule still shows detergent cleaning only.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not assume the old method still applies. Ask your supervisor for the updated instruction in writing, and follow it. The principle is that the schedule changes with the known organism.

equipmentAndPpe: Copy of the current cleaning schedule
Task record sheet or electronic log
Disposable gloves for the tasks listed

commonErrors.error: Working from an outdated copy of the schedule.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the issue date as each shift begins, and ask if the copy is stale.

commonErrors.error: Changing a frequency because a task seems unnecessary.
commonErrors.prevention: Raise it with the supervisor. Frequencies are set by the facility's risk assessment.

commonErrors.error: Recording tasks from memory at the close of the shift.
commonErrors.prevention: Record each task when it is completed, against its schedule line.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: If an outbreak notice changes a product or method, follow the written change. Do not substitute a stronger product without authorisation.

qualityStandard: Learner can point to the current schedule and state its issue date.
Learner names the four elements an outsourced service must document.
Records match the schedule line by line.
documentationEvidence: Task log checked against the current schedule
Written notice of any schedule change, with the date it was received
summary: A written schedule sets responsibility, roster, frequency and product for each area.
Outsourced cleaning must document its frequencies, staffing, equipment and management.
A known microbe triggers a timetable change, and the change arrives in writing.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which set of items must a written cleaning schedule contain?
options: Only the names of the cleaners and their shift times and their days off
Responsibilities, the roster, the frequency of each task and the products to use.
The hourly pay rates of each cleaner and the bonus each one is paid for the year
Only the times the building opens and closes and the lift servicing dates

knowledgeChecks.question: Which four elements must an outsourced cleaning service document?
options: Frequencies and methods, staffing, equipment and consumables, and on-site management.
Brand names of the cleaners, their phone numbers, their uniforms and their car parks.
Only the price of each cleaning task and the cleaner's own hourly rate and tax
Just the total hours logged across the week and the total pay for the week

knowledgeChecks.question: How does the timetable respond once a known microbe is present?
options: Nothing changes, and the schedule is left as it was first written down
The schedule is adjusted for that agent, as the facility's risk assessment directs.
Cleaners stop working in the affected area until the area is reopened by the manager
Cleaners clean the area only once a year and only on the first day of spring
